title: GlobalFoundries to make key AI chip component for TSMC in $2 billion deal
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

GlobalFoundries has agreed to manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC under a five-year, $2 billion deal announced on October 8. Production will take place at GlobalFoundries’ Malta, New York, facility, with volume manufacturing expected to start ramping in the first half of 2028. The agreement will support TSMC’s CoWoS advanced packaging ecosystem, which helps assemble powerful AI computing systems.

Silicon interposers are essential connectors inside these systems. They sit beneath processors and memory chips, providing dense pathways that allow data to move quickly between components. TSMC’s packaging technology brings computing chips and high-bandwidth memory together, helping deliver the performance needed for demanding AI workloads. As processors become more powerful, the connections surrounding them become increasingly important to overall system performance.

The deal matters because advanced packaging has become a significant constraint on AI chip production. Manufacturing more processors alone cannot solve the problem if companies lack the capacity to assemble them into finished products. Additional interposer supply could help TSMC address one part of that bottleneck and support future growth in AI hardware shipments. That is a potential benefit, rather than an immediate outcome: the planned production ramp remains more than a year away.

For GlobalFoundries, the agreement creates a substantial role in the AI supply chain through specialized manufacturing. For TSMC, it establishes an additional American source for an important packaging component. GlobalFoundries says Malta is expected to become the first U.S. source of silicon interposers for advanced packaging.

The broader implication is that AI infrastructure depends on an interconnected manufacturing ecosystem. This agreement suggests opportunities extend beyond processor fabrication to the components that make complete systems work. Its eventual impact will depend on successful production, sufficient demand and whether other supply constraints can also be eased as the industry expands capacity over time.
